analysis.one_liner: Makes every federal regulation expire automatically unless the agency completes a review and extends it.
analysis.headline: Introduced with seven Republican sponsors in March 1995, the bill was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put an expiration date on every federal regulation: existing rules would die seven years after enactment and new rules five years after taking effect, unless the issuing agency formally reviewed the rule, took comments from the White House budget office and Congress, and published a notice extending it [S2] [S3]. Agencies would have to judge each rule against 18 criteria weighing costs, competition, and burden on industry [S3]. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal regulation. Under the bill, a rule's effectiveness would end on its termination date unless the agency completed the full review-and-extension process, so a missed deadline or an unfavorable review would wipe out a requirement without any vote in Congress [S3]. The review criteria also direct agencies to consider how rules impede competition, reduce information requirements (especially for small businesses), and impose the minimum economic burdens necessary [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires each agency to systematically review all of its regulations to find those that are obsolete, inconsistent, duplicative, or impede competition, and to recommend terminating, extending, modifying, or consolidating them [S2] [S3].
Puts the White House budget office (the OIRA Administrator) in the middle of every review, with authority to send comments agencies must consider before deciding whether a rule survives [S2] [S3].
Requires agencies to publish solicitations for comments from the public, including the private sector, before making termination or extension decisions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections. Rules covering health, safety, the environment, and finance would lose force automatically unless agencies acted in time, and decisions to extend would be made by agency heads under White House budget-office review rather than by Congress. Court challenges to a termination or extension would be limited to a 30-day window and to a narrow type of review [S3], and the normal public notice-and-comment process would not apply to extensions or modifications [S3].

drawbacks.text: Making expiration the default is risky: the bill terminates a regulation's effectiveness unless the agency completes a multi-step review, preliminary report, comment period, final report, and extension notice within set deadlines [S3], so an agency that misses a step would let a rule die even if it still protects public health and safety.

The bill strips ordinary notice-and-comment procedures from extensions and modifications of regulations [S3] and limits lawsuits over those decisions to a 30-day window under a narrow standard of review [S3], reducing the public's ability to challenge a decision to let a rule lapse.

A good-faith case for the bill: federal rules accumulate for decades and many become obsolete or duplicative, and mandatory review with public comment and cost-benefit criteria could improve the quality of regulation without any rule actually expiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Regular, public review of old regulations is a reasonable goal, and several provisions (public comment, cost-benefit criteria, consolidating duplicative rules) point that way. But the bill's core mechanism inverts the burden of proof: instead of repealing a bad rule through a deliberate process, every rule expires by default unless the agency saves it under deadline pressure, with the White House budget office weighing in and the public's day in court sharply limited [S3]. A rule that still protects people could vanish because of paperwork timing, and there is no special protection for high-stakes health, safety, or environmental rules. The design would create leverage for regulated industries without a comparable safeguard for the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never reported it out, so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Domenici, joined by Sen. Spencer Abraham, introduced the bill on March 7, 1995; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Six Republican senators signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referral — no hearings listed, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial rules are better off, because the automatic-expiration scheme never became law. Agencies were also spared the cost of re-reviewing every regulation on a fixed clock.

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Regulatory Sunset and Review Act of 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: Senate committee to which the bill was referred (chair: Sen. William Roth, R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 7, 1995 and never reported it out; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Republicans and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no record of how the parties would have split on the merits.

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (manufacturing, energy, financial firms, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill makes expiration the default for every federal regulation unless an agency affirmatively extends it, which would give regulated businesses standing leverage against rules they dislike — a missed deadline ends a requirement with no vote by Congress. The review criteria explicitly weight competition, cost, and burden on industry [S3]. The public interest in those rules runs the other way.

industries.industry: Small businesses with federal reporting requirements
industries.note: The review criteria direct agencies to consider reducing information requirements, particularly for small businesses [S3]. Small firms would benefit from lighter paperwork whether or not the underlying rules serve the public.

industries.industry: Office of Management and Budget (Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs)
industries.note: The bill routes every regulation review through the OIRA Administrator, who must evaluate agency reports and transmit recommendations agencies must consider [S2] [S3]. That would cement White House budget-office control over which rules survive, regardless of the outcome for any single rule.
